Title: Mucinous differentiation does not impact stage or risk of recurrence among patients with grade 1, endometrioid type, endometrial carcinoma.

Journal/Date: Gynecologic oncology (2014)

MeSH Keywords: Adenocarcinoma, Mucinous, Aged, Carcinoma, Endometrioid, Cell Differentiation, Cohort Studies, Endometrial Neoplasms, Female, Humans


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVE]: To evaluate whether the presence of mucinous differentiation influences histopathologic findings, stage distribution, or rate of recurrence among women with grade 1, endometrioid type, endometrial carcinoma.
[METHODS]: This was a retrospective cohort study of all patients with grade 1, endometrioid type, endometrial carcinoma between January 2005 and December 2012. Patients were separated by the presence or absence of mucinous differentiation and then compared.
[RESULTS]: Of 655 patients, mucinous differentiation was present in 137 (20.9%) and absent in 518 (79.1%) patients. Compared to the group without mucinous differentiation, the group containing mucinous differentiation was older at diagnosis (mean: 61.1 vs. 58.5 years, OR, 95% CI; 1.03, 1.01-1.05) and more likely to have myometrial invasion (61.3% vs. 51.5%, OR, 95% CI; 1.49, 1.01-2.19). Additional histopathologic findings including: tumor size, cervical stromal invasion, adnexal involvement, LVI and/or the presence of positive lymph nodes were similar between groups. Mucinous differentiation did not affect stage distribution, as most patients were stage 1A (85.4% vs. 86.3%). The median PFS for the entire group has yet to be reached. The mean PFS for the entire study sample was 94.7 months. There was no difference in mean PFS when comparing the group with mucinous differentiation to the group without mucinous differentiation (98 vs. 93.4 months, p=0.07).
[CONCLUSIONS]: In the setting of grade 1, endometrioid type, endometrial carcinoma, mucinous differentiation is more common in older patients and is associated with an increased likelihood of myometrial invasion. However, stage distribution and risk of recurrence are not affected.

key_findings.finding: The most directly relevant study is a retrospective cohort of 655 patients specifically with FIGO grade 1 endometrioid-type endometrial carcinoma: 137 (20.9%) had mucinous differentiation and 518 did not. Mucinous differentiation was associated with older age (mean 61.1 vs 58.5 years) and more myometrial invasion (61.3% vs 51.5%; OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.01–2.19), but not with FIGO stage distribution: stage IA predominated similarly (85.4% vs 86.3%).

source_tools.relevance: Direct abstract of the grade-1 endometrioid cohort

key_findings.finding: In the same grade-1 cohort, mucinous differentiation was not associated with recurrence risk or progression-free survival. Mean PFS was 98 months with mucinous differentiation versus 93.4 months without; the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.07). The abstract reports no adjusted survival model, so it does not establish whether the null association persists after adjustment for age, myometrial invasion, LVSI, stage, or other covariates.

source_tools.relevance: Direct PFS and recurrence results plus limitation on adjustment

key_findings.finding: A separate single-institution case-control study evaluated 41 predominantly mucinous endometrial adenocarcinomas against age- and grade-matched endometrioid controls; it was not restricted to grade-1 endometrioid carcinomas with versus without mucinous differentiation and therefore is indirect for the requested comparison. It found more lymph-node metastases with mucinous histology (17% vs 3%, p=0.01), and mucinous histology remained an independent predictor after controlling for grade and depth of myometrial invasion (p=0.02), but there was no difference in recurrence rate or overall survival.

source_tools.relevance: Direct abstract of the distinct pure/predominantly mucinous versus endometrioid case-control study

key_findings.finding: The available evidence supports distinguishing pure/predominantly mucinous carcinoma from endometrioid carcinoma with mucinous differentiation: the 2014 study directly addresses the latter and shows no stage or recurrence/PFS disadvantage, whereas the 2012 study concerns predominantly mucinous histology and suggests higher nodal-metastasis risk despite similar recurrence and survival. No directly relevant cohort identified here reported disease-specific survival for grade-1 endometrioid carcinoma stratified by mucinous differentiation.
